claim: FireflySpace/fprime-topo-analysis (v0.1.0; 17 commits dated 2026-08-29 to 2026-09-14; author Will MacCormack; not peer-reviewed) is a static analyzer for F Prime. It joins the inter-component topology from fpp-to-json (each input port tagged sync, guarded or async) with intra-component handler-to-output-port flow recovered by libclang from compile_commands.json. Its about 15 checks include lock-order deadlock (self and ABBA), lock-aware member data races, async-queue producers, priorities and fill rates, unconnected ports, sync cycles, dead telemetry, buffer ownership and assert-taint reachability. Its README lists as non-goals user-written threads and callbacks (beyond the Os::Task routines it recovers), runtime guards (assumed taken) and run-time port routing. It assumes command registration happens single-threaded at startup. A grep of its source found no analysis of message ordering, staleness or freshness.

recheck.corrected_claim:
ROSDiscover (Timperley, Dürschmid, Schmerl, Garlan, Le Goues) appeared at ICSA 2022, not ICSE 2022: IEEE, pp. 112-123, DOI 10.1109/ICSA53651.2022.00019, per ROSInfer's reference list. The rosdiscover-evaluation README says "ICSA, 2021", which is most likely a year typo. ROSDiscover works from ROS 1 C++ source. It uses Clang ASTs, reachability analysis and symbolic function summaries to build component models: topic publish/subscribe ports, service ports (calls and provided services) and parameters. The paper says it focuses on "topic, service, and action ports", and parameters are modelled but not called ports. Launch files supply the system composition (nodes, parameters, remappings). Bug detection checks four first-order-logic well-formedness rules in Acme: one message-type mismatch rule and three variants of dangling publishers or subscribers using similar names or types. No ordering, startup or timing property is checked. The paper notes that domain experts could add more rules but did not explore this.

ROSInfer (ICSE 2024, DOI 10.1145/3597503.3639206) extends ROSDiscover. It infers component state machines statically from ROS C++ source. Input triggers are subscribed messages, periodic triggers, and component events such as "component started". State variables are found with two heuristics. The usage heuristic: the variable appears in the control conditions of architecturally relevant behaviour (functions that send messages, functions that change state variables, and their transitive callers). The scope heuristic: the variable is global or component-wide. State changes are inferred from assignments to these variables, with triggers inferred the same way. The paper does not require the assignment to be in a subscriber callback. The code at rosdiscover@78301b8, states_analyzer.py L30-42, requires an assignment in a function other than the publishing one; L53-68 then splits assignments into subscriber-callback and main-entry ones. ROSInfer emits PlusCal/TLA+ and checks user LTL properties or auto-generated "expected output eventually happens" properties. With a given component list, desired output and parameter assignments, it detected three known bugs from the ROSDiscover dataset that ROSDiscover could not find (autoware-02, -03, -10). In each, a required input is not connected to any publisher, so the component waits indefinitely. It does not model message contents ("we do not model the content of messages"). In future work the authors note that static analysis cannot infer execution times, so its models "cannot be used for most kinds of performance analysis, bottleneck analysis, or analysis of race condition". scope.corrected_claim:
ROSDiscover was published at ICSA 2022 (19th IEEE ICSA, pp. 112-123, DOI 10.1109/ICSA53651.2022.00019), not ICSE 2022. It targets ROS 1 C++ code. It builds component models from Clang ASTs plus symbolic function summaries, and launch files supply the composition. The paper says it focuses on topic, service and action ports. It also recovers component parameters, which the Acme style models as parameter-service ports. The paper picks four topic rules: message-type mismatch and three dangling publisher/subscriber heuristics. The ROSFam.acme it ships also has other structural rules: no service or action call to self, parameter reader and writer existence, no duplicate nodes, one bus per topic, and nodelet grouping. None of these rules, in the paper or in ROSFam.acme, states an ordering, startup or timing property.

ROSInfer (ICSE 2024, DOI 10.1145/3597503.3639206) is an extension of ROSDiscover. It infers component state machines from ROS C++ code using ROS 1 APIs. Transitions are driven by subscriber callbacks, and the paper also lists service callbacks (advertiseService) and message_filters registerCallback. Periodic triggers (Rate/Timer/sleep loops) and component events such as "component started" also drive transitions. The paper's state-variable heuristics are:
- the variable is global or component-scoped;
- it is used in control conditions of architecturally relevant behaviour (message-sending code, state-changing code and their transitive callers).

In the rosdiscover code at commit 78301b86, a state variable is one that appears in a publish call's inter-procedural condition and is assigned in some function other than the publishing one. Assignment does not have to happen in a subscriber callback; assignments are then split into subscriber-callback and main/entry-point groups. ROSInfer generates PlusCal/TLA+. Users either give LTL properties or a list of expected outputs, from which it auto-generates LTL properties. Applied to three already-known Autoware bugs from the ROSDiscover dataset (autoware-02, -03, -10), with a given component list, desired output and parameter values, it detected all three. In each, a required input has no publisher. Its formalism states 'we do not model the content of messages'. In future work the authors say static analysis cannot infer execution times, 'producing models that cannot be used for most kinds of performance analysis, bottleneck analysis, or analysis of race condition'. Both papers name NASA F Prime as a framework the approach could generalize to.

claim: TaxDC (Leesatapornwongsa et al., ASPLOS 2016, DOI 10.1145/2872362.2872374) studies 104 distributed-concurrency bugs in Cassandra, HBase, Hadoop MapReduce and ZooKeeper. It defines a message-timing order violation as a bug that manifests whenever a message arrives earlier (or later) than another event, either a message or a local computation, but not in the other order; 44% of the bugs are of this kind. 64% of the bugs are triggered by untimely messages. Table 1 lists the error symptoms 'Global missing messages' and 'Global unexpected messages'. Its §8.4 proposes detecting such bugs by (1) obtaining timing specifications, i.e. order and atomicity specifications among messages and computation, and (2) detecting violations by static or dynamic analysis, with invariant templates such as 'message bc should arrive at C before message ac arrives'. It also gives concrete cases: m3274 (an early kill message is incorrectly ignored) and h5780 (a join request sent before the security-key message arrives makes initialization abort).

recheck.corrected_claim: TaxDC (Leesatapornwongsa, Lukman, Lu, Gunawi, ASPLOS '16; the PDF prints DOI 10.1145/2872362.2872374) studies 104 distributed-concurrency (DC) bugs: 19 Cassandra, 30 HBase, 36 Hadoop MapReduce and 19 ZooKeeper. These were randomly sampled from the CBS database, reported 2011-2014. Under 'Message Timing Bugs', §3.1 defines an order violation as 'a DC bug [that] manifests whenever a message comes earlier (later) than another event, which is another message or a local computation, but not when the message comes later (earlier)'. Table 2 counts 46 bugs (44%) caused only by order violations, 21 (20%) only by atomicity violations, and 4 (4%) by multiple timing conditions. Finding #1 says 64% of the bugs are triggered by untimely messages, 32% by untimely faults or reboots, and 4% by both. Table 1 lists 'Global missing messages' and 'Global unexpected messages' among the error symptoms (§4). §8.4 ('Bug Detection Tools', part of §8 'Lessons Learned') proposes a generic detection framework with two tasks: (1) obtain timing specifications, i.e. order and atomicity specifications among messages and computation; (2) detect violations of them through dynamic or static analysis. It offers invariant templates such as 'message bc should arrive at C before message ac (ca) arrives (leaves)'. It also proposes error-guided inference, where program analysis infers timing specifications backward from explicit error checks. This is a proposal with no implementation or evaluation in the paper. The paper gives two cases. In m3274 a task-kill message (ac_kill) arrives at the NodeManager before the task-init message (bc_init) and is incorrectly ignored. In h5780 a region server sends its cluster-join request (bc_join) before the security-key message from ZooKeeper (ab_key) arrives, which aborts initialization; this is a race between a message arrival and a message send.

scope.reasoning:
I checked every part of the claim against the full text of the PDF. The PDF is the authors' self-hosted copy, and its hash matches the claim. Each statement is supported and the cited line numbers are right. The 44% figure is precisely 'caused only by ordering violations' (46 of 104 bugs). The 64% figure is Finding #1's 'untimely messages', which is the 44% plus the 20% atomicity bugs. Both are stated correctly. Nothing is generalized from an abstract, and none of it reaches beyond TaxDC's own text, so I do not refute the claim.

The claim needs three precision fixes.
(a) §8.4 sits in the 'Lessons Learned' discussion. It describes a direction ('should focus on', 'future DC bug detection'). It does not build or evaluate a detector, and 'proposes' should not be read as a working method.
(b) The invariant templates come from a separate 'Invariant-guided detection' paragraph about learned likely invariants, not from the two-step framework itself.
(c) TaxDC's model is shared-nothing datacenter nodes. Its statistics (the paper warns against generalizing them, lines 380-385) describe four Apache systems.

The why_central inference goes further than the evidence, though the claim itself does not.
First, TaxDC anticipates only the general decomposition: get an order specification, then detect violations of it statically or dynamically. It does not formulate the specific conjunction RequiredHB ∧ ¬ProvenHB ∧ PotentialConcurrent, and it does not define any static happens-before analysis. 'The core formula is not new' is therefore too strong. The supportable wording is that 'the specification-plus-violation-detection framing is anticipated by TaxDC §8.4, as a proposed direction'.
Second, 'F1 and F5 must be restated as instances of' TaxDC's class is also too strong. cFS apps run inside a single cFE instance, which does not match TaxDC's shared-nothing nodes, so the mapping is an analogy (inference). F1 (publish before the subscriber is ready) is analogous to a message-compute order violation like m3274. F5 (a consumer starts before its provider is initialized) matches TaxDC's message-timing class only when the dependency goes through a message, as in h5780. Otherwise it is closer to a local, LC-style order violation. The note should cite TaxDC as the closest established taxonomy and describe F1 and F5 as analogous to it, not as instances of it.

Its definition of order violation is a message-timing condition: a DC bug that manifests whenever a message comes earlier (later) than another event, either another message or a local computation, but not when the message comes later (earlier). 46 bugs (44%) are caused only by order violations; 4 more bugs (4%) have mixed timing conditions. In §4.1/Table 3 these are called 'wrong messages': the receiver gets an incorrect message from the triggering node and throws an exception (29%). claim: Burrows and Leino (author manuscript krml107, published in Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 16(12), 2004, DOI 10.1002/cpe.866) define a stale-value error as reading a shared variable while holding a lock and later using the value when the lock is no longer held. Such an error can occur even when every shared access is lock-protected. Their annotation-free compile-time checker in ESC/Java uses ghost booleans (stale_t, from_critical_t) per local variable and mostly ignores which lock is acquired. On about 617 kloc it reported 43 false alarms, 1 benign race and 4 bugs. Their staleness is relative to critical-section boundaries, not to physical age or to whether the producer has published a newer value.
evidence: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/krml107.pdf
why_central: This is the direct static-analysis precedent for the note's F3 'stale state' category. Its exact scope (sync-scope staleness, not message epoch or time) decides whether F3 freshness can still be framed as an open question.

recheck.corrected_claim:
Burrows and Leino, "Finding Stale-Value Errors in Concurrent Programs". The author manuscript is krml107. Microsoft Research's page gives the venue as Concurrency and Computation: Practice & Experience, vol. 16, October 2004, pp. 1161-1172, and links the issue DOI 10.1002/cpe.v16:12. MSR's own BibTeX says number={2}, which conflicts with that. The article DOI 10.1002/cpe.866 could not be checked because doi.org, Crossref and Wiley were blocked.

In the introduction the paper loosely describes the error as a value read from a shared variable while a lock is held but not held when the value is later used. It says this can happen even when every shared-variable access is correctly lock-protected.

The technique and the examples are narrower than that. Using a snapshot after leaving the critical section is called "justifiable" and is not flagged. A local variable last assigned inside a critical section becomes stale only when the thread enters another critical section. That includes re-entry after wait(), where the stale use can happen while the lock is held again. Every later read of that variable is then flagged.

The ESC/Java extension needs no annotations. It adds ghost booleans stale_t and from_critical_t for each local variable only (not formal parameters or temporaries). It mostly ignores which lock is acquired, with special handling for calls to synchronized methods of the same abstraction.

On 8 Java programs totalling 617 kloc it reported 48 warnings: 43 false alarms, 1 benign race and 4 previously unknown bugs. The authors say they are unsure how the ambit and jigsaw warnings should be categorized.

Inference: staleness here is counted in critical-section entries (J0/J1/G2, and the proposed age_t counter J2). It does not measure physical time or check whether a producer actually published a newer value.

Staleness is counted in critical-section entries. counter.corrected_claim:
Burrows and Leino, "Finding stale-value errors in concurrent programs", first appeared as Compaq SRC Technical Note 2002-004 (14 May 2002). An ACM DL-derived reference lists the journal version as Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 16(12):1161-1172, October 2004, with issue DOI 10.1002/cpe.v16:12. The article DOI 10.1002/cpe.866 could not be resolved here. krml107 is a lightly revised manuscript of the same paper (the 2002 note has the same results table). It was not checked against the Wiley version.

The paper targets an error that "can occur even when each shared-variable access is correctly protected by a lock". The introduction words it as a lock held when the value is read but not when it is later used. The rule the checker actually applies (Sections 1-2) is different:
- Using the snapshot outside the critical section right after the read (t1 := t0) is called "justifiable" and is not flagged.
- What gets flagged is reading a local variable whose last assignment happened inside a critical section, after a later critical-section entry (ghost statement G2). This includes uses made while the lock is held again. Their main producer/consumer bug uses the stale array copy after wait() has re-acquired the lock.

The checker is an annotation-free extension of ESC/Java. It adds ghost booleans stale_t and from_critical_t for each local variable (locals only, not formal parameters or ESC temporaries). from_critical_t marks any assignment made inside a critical section, not only reads of shared variables. The checker mostly ignores which lock is acquired. The exceptions are calls to synchronized methods of the same abstraction and wait(), which is modelled as re-entry.

scope.corrected_claim:
Burrows and Leino, "Finding stale-value errors in concurrent programs" (author manuscript krml107.pdf, Compaq SRC affiliation). The MSR publication page lists it as Concurrency and Computation: Practice & Experience, October 2004, and links the issue DOI 10.1002/cpe.v16:12. The MSR BibTeX gives vol. 16, pp. 1161-1172, but number = 2, which is inconsistent with the issue link. I could not resolve the article DOI 10.1002/cpe.866, and I did not compare the published text with the manuscript; only the abstracts were seen to match.

The paper is about stale-value errors. A value is read from a shared variable inside one critical section and then used after the thread has left that section and entered a later one, including re-acquiring the lock after wait(). Other threads may have updated the variable in between. The introduction's informal wording is "lock held when read, not held when later used". However, the paper says that simply using the snapshot outside a critical section is "justifiable" and is not flagged. Only uses after a later critical-section entry are flagged. Such errors can occur even when every shared-variable access is correctly lock-protected.

The checker is a compile-time extension of ESC/Java and needs no annotations. It adds ghost booleans stale_t and from_critical_t for each local variable. Only locals are covered, not formal parameters or ESC temporaries, and the implementation assigns an arbitrary value instead of true. It mostly ignores which lock is acquired, except at calls to synchronized methods of the same abstraction.

On 8 Java programs totalling 617 kloc it produced 48 warnings: 43 false alarms, 1 benign race and 4 previously unknown bugs. The authors say they are unsure of the categorization for ambit and jigsaw. The checker's staleness depends only on critical-section re-entry, as a conservative stand-in for "another thread may have written a newer value". It does not check whether a write actually happened, and it tracks no version, epoch or physical time. The proposed future age_t counter counts critical-section entries, not time.

scope.reasoning:
Most of the claim is accurate. I checked it against the full manuscript text, with an independent stream extraction of a hash-identical PDF. Accurate parts: the 'even when every shared access is lock-protected' statement, the annotation-free ESC/Java checker, the per-local ghost booleans stale_t/from_critical_t, 'mostly ignores which lock', and the totals of 617 kloc, 43 false alarms, 1 benign race and 4 bugs. Overreach and imprecision:
(1) The definition 'later using the value when the lock is no longer held' copies the paper's informal intro sentence, but it is broader than what the paper actually defines and detects. The paper explicitly calls using a snapshot after release 'justifiable' and does not flag it. Warnings come only after a later critical-section entry, such as re-acquisition after wait(), and in that case the lock IS held at use time. For the note's F3 framing, the boundary that matters is the re-entry or re-acquisition boundary, not simply 'after release'.
(2) The claim says staleness is not tied to whether the producer published a newer value. That is right for the detector, which never tracks actual writes. But the paper's concept is motivated by possible intervening writes by other threads, so the checker should be described as a conservative re-entry proxy for 'possibly superseded', not as unrelated to newer writes.
(3) The results omit two caveats: the authors say they are unsure of the categorization for ambit and jigsaw (the benign race and 22 false alarms come from those two programs), and the implementation covers only locals.
(4) The bibliographic details are stated as checked fact, but the manuscript carries no venue information. The MSR page supports 'CCPE, October 2004, issue v16:12', while its own BibTeX says number 2. I could not resolve the article DOI cpe.866, and I did not check the published body text against the manuscript.

The code's checker enum confirms that IKOS has no ordering or concurrency checker, so 'only' is justified at this commit. TROUBLESHOOTING.md L94-96 is even stronger, more direct evidence than the README assumption.

The claim is imprecise in four places:
(a) It leaves out the unaligned-pointer checker, and it calls dead code, the soundness check and the assertion prover 'runtime-error properties' when they are not.
(b) It does not say that unsigned overflow and pointer overflow are off by default. The assertion prover can check user-written invariants, so 'only runtime-error properties' applies to the built-in checkers only.
(c) The BioSentinel and CFE-model numbers can only be traced to a paraphrased search snippet recorded by an earlier agent. NTRS is blocked, so they cannot be checked. The claim does hedge with 'per a search snippet', but it drops 'average' from the warning rate. Its why_central also uses the ~1200 LOC figure to estimate modelling effort, which unverified figures should not support.
(d) Here the why_central overreaches. It calls the single-thread and extern-globals assumptions 'the stated reason it cannot see SB-delivered state', but IKOS's docs never mention cFS or the SB. Also, once a CFE framework model supplies function bodies, CFE API calls are no longer body-less extern functions, so L538 does not by itself explain anything about SB-delivered state. That link is our inference, and it is uncertain.

The core factual claim is correct, so I set refuted=false. The narrower wording above fixes (a) to (d).

recheck.reasoning:
I re-opened every cited source at the cited refs. Most of the claim checks out: arinc.ml and osek.ml exist at v1.1.0 with the quoted or described content, both are gone at v2.0.0 (the CHANGELOG confirms they were removed there), the HEAD READMEs say what is quoted, and the MHP domain fields and definitely_not_started logic are as described. Two concrete errors still make the claim as stated false, and one of them weakens its why_central argument.

(1) 'Neither file exists at v1.0.0 (HTTP 404)' is wrong. The repo has no v1.0.0 tag, so any raw URL under v1.0.0 returns 404, README.md included. The real 1.0.0 release tag is 'goblint-1.0.0', and both arinc.ml and osek.ml exist there, as they do at svcomp21/22 and v0.9.8-pre_cleaning. The files did not first appear in v1.1.0. They existed for years and were removed in v2.0.0.

(2) 'Handles ... Create/Send/ReceiveQueuingMessage, Write/ReadSamplingMessage, ... buffers' overstates the code. Those calls are pattern-matched but mapped to todo(), which adds a Nop action. Only processes, blackboards, semaphores, events, timed waits and the error handler become model actions for the graph and Promela output. ARINC's message-passing IPC, the closest analogue to the cFS Software Bus, is therefore not extracted. This narrows the why_central framing: the prior art recovered process, synchronisation and blackboard semantics from C into Promela or dot, but not queuing/sampling message flow. It is still relevant prior art for 'recovering RTOS API semantics from C', but not for message-ordering extraction. Also, osek.ml describes itself as a shared-memory data race analysis.

Minor imprecisions: a8a2e9c4 is the annotated tag object (the commit is 5e1a53e2). 'Create/Send/ReceiveQueuingMessage' should read CreateQueuingPort/Send/ReceiveQueuingMessage. The timeout variants are only SuspendSelf, ReadBlackboard, WaitSemaphore and WaitEvent, with 'TODO timeout' comments. The removal notice comes from two READMEs (14-osek and 17-arinc), one per feature; the claim attributes both to the cited 17-arinc README, which mentions only ARINC. The mHP line ranges are off by about one line.

counter.corrected_claim: Goblint's annotated tag v1.1.0 (tag object a8a2e9c4, commit 5e1a53e2c87660f8be8a3bbd43b64075fc15233d, 2021-11-26) contains src/analyses/arinc.ml. The file's header reads "Tracking of arinc processes and their actions. Output to console, graphviz and promela." The analysis recognizes the whole LAP_Se_* ARINC 653 APEX call list, but its transfer function turns only some calls into modelled actions, which feed the dot and Promela output: process creation, start/stop/suspend/resume, preemption lock and unlock, partition mode, blackboards (intra-partition messages), semaphores, events, TimedWait/PeriodicWait and the error handler. Sampling-port and queuing-port calls (Create*Port, Write/ReadSamplingMessage, Send/ReceiveQueuingMessage) and buffer calls go through todo() and become Nop. The action type has no constructor for them, and a code comment says queuing messages and buffers are left out because they "don't affect the status of the modelled system (e.g. communication with outside)". The same tag contains src/analyses/osek.ml ("Data race analysis for OSEK programs."). It parses OIL files, computes ceiling priorities, tracks ISRs, and treats DisableAllInterrupts, SuspendAllInterrupts, SuspendOSInterrupts and RES_SCHEDULER as pseudo-resources. These analyses predate 1.1.0. There is no v1.0.0 tag; the 1.0.0 release tag goblint-1.0.0 (c50ee911, 2017-12-07) already contains both files, and osek.ml exists back to v0.9.5 (2011). At HEAD (d0ee7d5b), two separate regression-test READMEs (14-osek, 17-arinc) say that OSEK, and separately ARINC653, support "has been removed from recent Goblint versions, please use Release 1.1.1". scope.reasoning:
Several parts of the claim check out against the primary source. The arinc.ml header text is correct. osek.ml does handle OSEK resources, compute ceiling priorities, map ISR IDs and treat DisableAllInterrupts as a pseudo-resource. Both files are absent at v2.0.0. The HEAD README says ARINC653 support was removed. The MHP domain fields are as described.

Two parts overreach, and both matter for the novelty argument this claim supports.

(1) The claim that "neither file exists at v1.0.0 (HTTP 404)" rests on a ref that does not exist. Goblint has no v1.0.0 tag, so the 404 says nothing about the files. The real 1.0.0 tag, goblint-1.0.0 (2017-12-07), contains both arinc.ml and osek.ml, and osek.ml already exists at v0.9.5 (2011). The wording implies the ARINC/OSEK support first appeared around v1.1.0. In fact it is older and lasted until it was removed somewhere between v1.1.1 (2021-11-29) and v2.0.0 (2022-08-18).

(2) The list of handled APEX calls goes beyond what the code does. Saying it handles "Create/Send/ReceiveQueuingMessage, Write/ReadSamplingMessage, ... buffers" is only true in the sense that the names are recognised. Every sampling-port, queuing-port and buffer call goes to todo(), which adds a Nop action. The action type has no constructor for these calls, the Promela extraction table does not register them, and arincUtil.ml says explicitly that they were left out because they are "communication with outside". (There is also no API called CreateQueuingMessage; the call is CreateQueuingPort.)

This is the most relevant point for why_central. The why_central text says Goblint 'extracted avionics RTOS inter-process communication into Promela or graph models', but the evidence supports something narrower. Goblint recovered RTOS process lifecycle and intra-partition synchronisation (semaphores, events, blackboard operations as events, and timeouts) from C by recognising API calls, and exported graphviz/Promela models. It did not model inter-partition message-port dataflow, which is the closest analogue to the cFS Software Bus. The prior-art point still holds as a general method: recognising RTOS API calls in C and exporting a process/synchronisation model. But it should not be described as message-IPC semantics recovery.

There are also smaller precision problems. a8a2e9c4 is the annotated tag object, not the commit; the commit is 5e1a53e2. The cited 17-arinc README covers only ARINC653, and the OSEK removal statement is in 14-osek/README.md. The definitely_not_started exclusion applies only to threads the current thread must be an ancestor of (descendants it has not yet transitively created), not to every thread not yet created.

recheck.corrected_claim:
At cFE 546a0025, a failed local SB delivery never shows up in the publisher's return code. Each part holds with these qualifications.

(a) A transmit on a MID that has no SB route returns CFE_SUCCESS. A route exists only after some Subscribe, SubscribeEx or SubscribeLocal call has created it since SB init. The send increments the uint8 HK NoSubscribersCounter and requests CFE_SB_SEND_NO_SUBS_EID (INFORMATION). The event is actually emitted only if two conditions hold:
- SB's single FIRST_4_STOP filter for EID 14 is not yet used up. This filter belongs to the SB app and is shared by every MID and sender since boot. In the native sample boot, core-app startup uses 3 of the 4 before any app runs.
- The publishing app is registered with EVS and has INFORMATION events enabled. EVS_IsFiltered calls CFE_EVS_GetTypeEnable, which looks up the calling task's AppId, not SB's.

(b) Routes are never removed. Unsubscribe and DeletePipe only unlink destination nodes. When a route exists but has zero destinations, a send produces no counter and no event and returns CFE_SUCCESS. When IsOrigination=true it also still advances the per-route sequence counter.

(c) A message is dropped for that pipe only in two cases:
- MsgLim is reached (BuffCount >= MsgLim). MsgLim caps how many messages of that MID can sit unread in that pipe; CFE_SB_Subscribe sets it to 4 by default.
- The OS queue is full (OS_QUEUE_FULL).
In either case MsgLimitErrorCounter or PipeOverflowErrorCounter increments, MsgSendErrorCounter also increments, and an ERROR event is requested (FIRST_16_STOP filter, gated by the same publisher event-type check). TransmitMsg still returns CFE_SUCCESS. sb_sendrecv_test.c asserts CFE_SUCCESS for the MsgLim case (L103-L107 with L166-L168). It asserts the same for MsgLim and pipe-depth drops in TestMsgBroadcast (L242-L250, L300-L304).

(d) CFE_SB_Qos_t is documented as currently unused and intended for interprocessor communication. Quality is only copied into the subscription report, and only when reporting is enabled. SB has no durability, latching or last-value retention: a route entry holds only the destination list, MsgId and SeqCnt, and a new subscription starts empty.

- T2: sequence count went 1 -> 5 across 3 sends with zero destinations.

recheck.reasoning:
I checked every cited source at the pinned SHA. Each one says what the claim attributes to it:
- No route: the counter increments, the NO_SUBS event is requested, and the status stays CFE_SUCCESS.
- Routes are never removed.
- With zero destinations a send produces no counter and no event, and the sequence counter still advances.
- MsgLim and pipe-full drops are per pipe; they increment counters and the send still returns CFE_SUCCESS.
- The QoS typedef is documented as unused, and Quality only reaches the subscription report.
- A route entry has no message storage.
- The probe numbers are quoted exactly from the logs.

So the core point holds: the publisher's return code never reveals a failed delivery, and the analyzer must reason about subscribe-versus-publish order itself. I do not refute the claim.

It is imprecise in five places:
1. It says the events are "raised" as if unconditionally. EVS_IsFiltered gates every event on CFE_EVS_GetTypeEnable, which reads the calling (publisher) task's AppId. A publisher that is not EVS-registered, or has INFORMATION/ERROR disabled, gets no NO_SUBS, MsgLim or Q_FULL event. This is why none of the five cited probe runs logged any such event: the probe never registered with EVS. I confirmed the mechanism by re-running with CFE_EVS_Register, and the events then appeared.
2. "Filtered after the first 4" is one SB-app-wide filter shared by every MID and sender since boot, not a per-MID budget. In the native sample boot, 3 of the 4 are used by core startup, and my re-run showed a second never-subscribed MID producing no event.
3. The sequence counter advances only when IsOrigination=true.
4. The cited test lines L103-L107 cover only the MsgLim case. The pipe-depth case is asserted at L242-L250 and L300-L304.
5. MsgLim and Q_FULL also increment MsgSendErrorCounter, and their events use FIRST_16_STOP, not FIRST_4_STOP.

The NoSub delta of 1 in the original probe partly depends on the probe being unregistered. With an EVS-registered publisher and nothing subscribed to the event MID 0x808, the first no-subscriber send gave a delta of 2.

Scope: I read the code and the functional test in full at the cited lines, plus the EVS paths involved. I re-ran the probe locally in an isolated IPC/mount namespace. I did not check EDS builds or non-default mission configurations.

scope.corrected_claim:
At cFE 546a0025, used with OSAL dad0ee99 and the default platform configuration, CFE_SB_TransmitMsg and CFE_SB_TransmitBuffer return CFE_SUCCESS whatever happens to individual destinations. They still return errors for caller-side faults: CFE_SB_BAD_ARGUMENT for a NULL pointer or invalid MsgId, CFE_SB_MSG_TOO_BIG, CFE_SB_BUF_ALOC_ERR, and a failed MSG origination action. The publisher's return code therefore cannot detect the following cases.

(a) No route exists for the MID because no pipe has subscribed to it since SB init. SB increments the uint8 NoSubscribersCounter and raises CFE_SB_SEND_NO_SUBS_EID. This is an INFORMATION event, filtered by default with FIRST_4_STOP, and the filter count covers all MIDs and senders together. MsgSendErrorCounter does not change. The call returns CFE_SUCCESS.

(b) In both shipped SBR map implementations (HASH and DIRECT), a route is never removed until the next SB init. After Unsubscribe or DeletePipe has removed every destination, a send produces no HK counter and no event and returns CFE_SUCCESS. For sends with IsOrigination=true it still advances the per-route sequence counter.

(c) If a destination is at its MsgLim, the message is dropped for that pipe only. The default for CFE_SB_Subscribe is CFE_PLATFORM_SB_DEFAULT_MSG_LIMIT = 4; SubscribeEx and SubscribeLocal take an explicit limit. A full queue or a queue write error also drops the message for that pipe only, because OS_QueuePut never blocks at this OSAL: its flags are "reserved/unused", and the POSIX, RTEMS and VxWorks backends send without waiting. TransmitBufferWithRoute's TimeOut therefore has no effect. In each case SB increments MsgLimitErrorCounter, or PipeOverflowErrorCounter or InternalErrorCounter. It also increments MsgSendErrorCounter and raises ERROR events. The default config filters MSGID_LIM_ERR and Q_FULL_ERR with FIRST_16_STOP. The call still returns CFE_SUCCESS. cFE's functional test sb_sendrecv_test.c asserts the CFE_SUCCESS return and the per-pipe drop for both the MsgLim case (L103-107, L165-168) and the pipe-depth case (TestMsgBroadcast, L206-296). It does not assert the counters or events. On Linux with the POSIX OSAL, the effective pipe depth can be silently truncated below the requested depth.

(d) CFE_SB_Qos_t is documented as currently unused; its fields are marked "currently unused". Within SB/SBR, Quality only reaches CFE_SB_SendSubscriptionReport. A code reading of SB/SBR found no durability, latching or last-value retention for late subscribers. This covers cFE SB only, not SBN or app-level re-publication.

- The sequence number advanced by 4 across 3 zero-destination origination sends plus one more send.
- MsgLim=2 with 5 sends gave 2 received, MsgLimitErrorCounter +3, MsgSendErrorCounter +3, and all return codes 0.
- Depth 3 with 5 sends gave 3 received, PipeOverflowErrorCounter +2, and all return codes 0.

scope.reasoning:
I checked every sub-claim against the pinned cFE source and the local probe output; all are substantively correct. I set refuted=false because the problems are imprecision, not wrong facts. The overreach points are these:

1. The headline 'local Software Bus delivery fails silently from the publisher's point of view' is broader than the evidence. TransmitMsg does return error codes for caller-side faults (BAD_ARGUMENT, MSG_TOO_BIG, BUF_ALOC_ERR, origination-action failure). Only per-destination outcomes are masked as CFE_SUCCESS. 'Silently' is also relative: cases (a) and (c) produce HK counters and (filtered) events. Only (b) is fully silent, with no counter and no event.

2. In (b), the sequence counter advances only for IsOrigination=true sends (cfe_sb_priv.c L1058-1064).

3. In (c), the cited test lines L103-107 assert only the MsgLim return code. The file as a whole (TestMsgBroadcast) also asserts the pipe-depth drop and per-pipe isolation. Nothing in it asserts the counters or events, so 'asserts this' should be limited to the return code and the per-pipe drop.

4. The full-pipe drop depends on OSAL behaviour. OSAL dad0ee99 OS_QueuePut never blocks, which makes the claim true for all transmit APIs, including TransmitBufferWithRoute despite its TimeOut parameter. The OSAL dependence should be stated.

5. The probe results are from one platform (Linux native, POSIX OSAL), and the claim reports only measured values, so it does not overgeneralize. The values match all five runs exactly.

6. The absence of latching and durability rests on reading SB/SBR code, plus one consistent probe observation in T2. It is limited to cFE SB, not SBN or apps.

The defaults (MsgLim 4, FIRST_4_STOP, uint8 counter) are default_/CFGVAL configuration values. Calling them 'default' is accurate.

TransmitMsg returns non-success only for argument, size or buffer-allocation errors (CFE_SB_BAD_ARGUMENT, CFE_SB_MSG_TOO_BIG, CFE_SB_BUF_ALOC_ERR) or an origination-action failure, never for missing or overflowing receivers.

(a) If no route exists for the MID, the publish increments the uint8 NoSubscribersCounter and hands an INFORMATION event CFE_SB_SEND_NO_SUBS_EID to EVS, then returns CFE_SUCCESS. A route is created inside CFE_SB_SubscribeFull before the destination is added, and no route exists only if no subscribe attempt for that MID has reached CFE_SBR_AddRoute since SB init. Whether the event is actually emitted depends on three things: the SB filter (CFE_EVS_FIRST_4_STOP by default, counted per event ID for the SB app across all senders), SB squelch, and, at this commit, the event-type enable mask of the calling (publisher) app. CFE_EVS_GetTypeEnable uses CFE_ES_GetAppID(), so a publisher that is not registered with EVS produces no SB event at all.

(b) Routes are never removed at runtime; only re-initialization at reset clears them. After Unsubscribe or pipe deletion, sends on a route with zero destinations produce no counter, no event and CFE_SUCCESS. When IsOrigination is true they still advance the per-route sequence counter. Destinations disabled by the SB Disable-Route command are skipped in the same silent way.

(c) Exceeding MsgLim (CFE_PLATFORM_SB_DEFAULT_MSG_LIMIT = 4, used by CFE_SB_Subscribe; SubscribeEx sets it per subscription), or a full pipe in the default POLL mode, drops the message for that pipe only. It increments MsgLimitErrorCounter or PipeOverflowErrorCounter, MsgSendErrorCounter and the pipe's SendErrors, and offers the ERROR events 17 or 25 (FIRST_16_STOP by default). TransmitMsg still returns CFE_SUCCESS. The functional test sb_sendrecv_test.c asserts this for the MsgLim case. The pipe-overflow case is asserted in the unit test sb_UT.c.

(d) CFE_SB_Qos_t is documented as currently unused. Quality only reaches the subscription report, and only when reporting is enabled. SB offers no durability, latching, last-value retention or delivery confirmation, and the docs state there is no built-in delivery confirmation and nothing is preserved across resets.

CFE_SB_TransmitTxn_FindDestinations then takes the SB mutex (priv L1049) and looks up the route. Only if the route is valid AND IsOrigination is true does it increment the per-route sequence counter and write it into the copy (L1058-1064). It walks the destination list from its head (L1067). Inactive destinations and IGNOREMINE self-pipes are skipped, and destinations over MsgLim are marked as errors. CFE_SB_AddDestNode inserts new subscriptions at the head (priv L361-391), and cfe_sb.h L238-244 says 'the message will first be sent to the last subscriber'. The mutex is released at L1114. CFE_MSG_OriginationAction (timestamp/checksum) runs next. OS_QueuePut is then called without the lock, once per recorded destination pipe that passed the MsgLim check (L1187-1188); the lock is retaken only to undo accounting when a put fails. cfe_sb.h L420-422 says a pending, subscribed higher-priority task 'may get to run before returning control to the caller'. On Linux, OSAL dad0ee99 posix OS_QueuePut_Impl calls mq_timedsend with constant priority 1 and a zeroed (already-expired) absolute timespec on a blocking queue. A full queue therefore returns ETIMEDOUT, which maps to OS_QUEUE_FULL: the message is dropped for that pipe, a counter is bumped, and TransmitMsg still returns success. Linux same-priority mqueue ordering makes each pipe FIFO in the order of the OS_QueuePut calls. Nothing orders delivery across pipes. scope.reasoning:
The core mechanics in the claim check out in the pinned source, and so do all the reported counts. Source lines confirmed: buffer copy, lock and route lookup, head-first walk, head insertion and the doc quote, unlock before OS_QueuePut, the cfe_sb.h preemption note, and mq_timedsend with priority 1, zero timeout and ETIMEDOUT mapped to QUEUE_FULL. Several statements are broader than the evidence, though:
(1) The sequence counter is said to be incremented unconditionally. It increments only when IsOrigination is true and the route is valid, which matters for relays and forwarders that pass false.
(2) 'OS_QueuePut once per destination pipe' leaves out the Active, IGNOREMINE, MaxPipes=16 and MsgLim filters. Destinations over MsgLim are dropped before any put, so SB has a second drop point besides the full OS queue.
(3) The 500/500 inversion was produced by one subscription order only: the relay pipe subscribed after the observer, so it is at the list head and written first. That order was never varied. Stated without the condition, the result reads as if any outranking relay inverts causality. From the code I infer that the reverse order would not invert on 1 CPU, but that was not tested.
(4) The 200/200 and 500/500 figures are per run, from two runs. The non-root numbers come from a single run, also on CPU 0 with msg_max=10, and its 'higher/lower' labels have no effect under SCHED_OTHER.
(5) The 0/500 on 4 CPUs is an observed timing outcome, not a guarantee. In that setup only 6/200 and 3/200 trials had all receivers run before TransmitMsg returned.
(6) CPU pinning is inferred from the log names and sched_getcpu snapshots; the pinning command itself is not recorded.

All measurements come from one Linux container kernel, and the per-pipe FIFO statement rests on Linux mqueue semantics only. The corrected claim adds these conditions.

counter.corrected_claim:
At cFE 546a0025 (still the cFE dev HEAD on 2026-10-01; cFE main 12cb84fc and v7.0.1 have the same structure), CFE_SB_TransmitMsg copies the message into a buffer from the SB pool. Under the SB mutex it looks up the route. When the route exists and IsOrigination is true, it also increments the per-route sequence counter, even if the route has no destinations left. It then walks the destination list from its head. Because Subscribe inserts new destinations at the head, cfe_sb.h and cfe_sb.dox say 'the message will first be sent to the last subscriber'. Under the lock it skips inactive destinations and IGNOREMINE self-pipes. It also drops any destination that is at its MsgLim; that drop only bumps a counter and produces no OS_QueuePut. The walk stops at CFE_PLATFORM_SB_MAX_DEST_PER_PKT entries. After unlocking, it runs CFE_MSG_OriginationAction (timestamp and checksum). It then calls OS_QueuePut without the mutex, once for each recorded pipe that did not hit MsgLim, and takes the mutex again only to undo the accounting when a put fails. cfe_sb.h says a higher-priority task that is pending and subscribed may run before TransmitMsg returns. On Linux the OSAL POSIX put calls mq_timedsend with constant priority 1 and an already-expired absolute timeout ({0,0}) on a blocking queue. Same-priority Linux mqueues are FIFO (checked in v6.18), so each pipe is FIFO in put order. A full queue returns ETIMEDOUT, which becomes OS_QUEUE_FULL: the message is dropped and only PipeOverflowErrorCounter changes, while TransmitMsg still returns CFE_SUCCESS. There is no order across pipes. Native-sim measurements (cFE 546a0025, OSAL dad0ee99, PSP 53df1d54, permissive mode compiled in):
- One CPU, SCHED_RR active (runs 1 and 5, 200 trials each): in every trial all 3 receivers, which ran at higher priority than the sender, ran before TransmitMsg returned, in reverse subscription order.
- Relay inversion: the relay's pipe was subscribed after the observer's, so it sat at the list head. When the relay outranked the sender, causality was inverted in 500/500 trials in each of runs 1 and 5. With a lower-priority relay it was 0/500.
- Four CPUs (runs 2 and 3): 0/500 inversions in both relay configurations. All 6 wake-order permutations occurred, and all three receivers ran before TransmitMsg returned in only 6/200 and 3/200 trials.
- Non-root, one CPU, msg_max=10 (one run, run 4): OSAL fell back to SCHED_OTHER. It returned no error and printed only an OS_DEBUG line. This run gave 15/500 and 30/500 inversions.
Version scope: placing the puts outside the mutex dates from cFE commit 550e7f7d (2024-02-26, 'refactor SB'), first released in tag v7.0.0. Earlier code called OS_QueuePut while holding the SB mutex: v6.7.0, draco-rc5/equuleus-rc1, and 550e7f7d's parent 9e5d452a. In that design one broadcast is atomic with respect to other SB transmits, so this relay-injection inversion should not occur there (inference, not measured). The channel model therefore has to be conditioned on the cFE version.

counter.reasoning:
I looked for counter-evidence in the pinned code, in later and earlier cFE versions, in OSAL configuration, in the Linux kernel source and in the probe's own method. None of it refutes the claim at its stated pin.

At the pin:
- I re-fetched every cited file. The hashes match and every cited line says what the claim says.
- Nothing newer supersedes it: cFE dev is still 546a0025, and main and v7.0.1 have the same lock-then-put-outside-lock structure.
- The Linux v6.18 mqueue source confirms same-priority FIFO and that the zero absolute timeout on a blocking queue returns ETIMEDOUT. Probe T4 confirms the drop-on-full path through PipeOverflowErrorCounter.
- The logs reproduce every number in the claim: runs 1 and 5 give 200/200 and 500/500 vs 0/500, runs 2 and 3 give 0/500 with 6 permutations, and run 4 gives 15/500 and 30/500.

The claim is imprecise in five places:
1. **Sequence counter:** it is incremented only when IsOrigination is true.
2. **Puts per pipe:** OS_QueuePut is not called for destinations over MsgLim, for inactive destinations or for IGNOREMINE self-pipes, and the destination count is capped. The origination action runs between the unlock and the puts.
3. **Inversion setup:** the 500/500 inversion depended on the relay's pipe being subscribed after the observer's, which puts it at the list head. The claim omits this condition.
4. **Non-root run:** it was a single run, pinned to one CPU with msg_max=10. "Silently" means no error is returned, but a debug line is printed.
5. **1-CPU results:** these come from two runs.

The most important counter-evidence is about versions. Before commit 550e7f7d (2024-02-26, first released in v7.0.0), cFE called OS_QueuePut while holding the SB mutex. This is the case in v6.7.0, in draco-rc5/equuleus-rc1 and in the commit's parent. In that design, a relay woken by the first put cannot transmit until the sender has finished every put. I infer that a broadcast was then effectively atomic with respect to other SB transmits and that the measured inversion would not occur, but I did not run this. This does not refute a claim pinned to 546a0025. It does mean the "channel model the analysis must use" has to depend on the cFE version, so I put that in the corrected claim.

What I could not check: VxWorks and RTEMS queue semantics, and an actual run of a pre-2024 cFE.

recheck.corrected_claim:
At cFE 546a0025, ES startup sync has a timeout and gives no readiness guarantee.
(a) CFE_ES_Main sets SystemState to EARLY_INIT, then CORE_STARTUP, CORE_READY, APPS_INIT and OPERATIONAL. It waits for every used app record to reach at least LATE_INIT, then RUNNING. Each wait uses CFE_PLATFORM_ES_STARTUP_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT_MSEC, which defaults to 1000 ms, is configurable, and is documented as a "soft limit"; it polls every 50 ms. On timeout ES only writes a syslog line and continues (cfe_es_start.c L204-229).
(b) For a non-core app, CFE_ES_WaitForSystemState first raises the caller's own AppState: OPERATIONAL becomes RUNNING, APPS_INIT becomes LATE_INIT and SHUTDOWN becomes STOPPED. A core app is raised to RUNNING for any state at or above CORE_READY. This raise happens before the wait, and it stays even if the wait later times out. The function then polls SystemState without the lock and returns CFE_ES_OPERATION_TIMED_OUT on timeout. The header states there is no option to wait indefinitely.
(c) CFE_ES_WaitForStartupSync is a void wrapper that drops this status. Its header says values below 1000 are rounded up, but neither the wrapper nor WaitForSystemState rounds; the value is passed through unchanged. Issue cFE #1466, which asks for a status return, is open. PR #2273 implemented it, was approved by jphickey and labelled CCB:Ready, and was then closed unmerged by its author on 2026-07-07. Upstream main still has the void signature.
(d) In a local native build of 546a0025, PROBE_SLOW made no ES sync call during a deliberate 2.5 s OS_TaskDelay. In all 4 scheduling configurations (R1-R4), ES logged both "Startup Sync failed" lines and entered OPERATIONAL. PROBE_LO and PROBE_HI then got CFE_SUCCESS from WaitForSystemState(OPERATIONAL,5000) after 1.95-2.005 s by the monotonic clock. That was about 0.5 s before PROBE_SLOW finished its delay. PROBE_SLOW was therefore not RUNNING when they returned; this is inferred from the probe code and the cFE code, not observed directly as a state value.

scope.corrected_claim:
At cFE 546a0025 (commit dated 2026-09-25), the startup synchronization for apps listed in the ES startup script is a soft, timeout-bounded wait. Reaching OPERATIONAL does not mean every startup-script app is RUNNING. The core apps are different: CFE_ES_CreateObjects waits up to CFE_PLATFORM_CORE_MAX_STARTUP_MSEC (default 30000 ms) for each core app to reach RUNNING and calls CFE_PSP_Panic if it does not (cfe_es_start.c L859-872).

(a) CFE_ES_Main moves SystemState from EARLY_INIT through CORE_STARTUP, CORE_READY, APPS_INIT and OPERATIONAL. It runs two separate waits, one for every in-use app record to reach LATE_INIT and one for RUNNING. Each wait is bounded by CFE_PLATFORM_ES_STARTUP_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT_MSEC, a mission-overridable platform parameter documented as a soft limit, with a default of 1000 ms (cfe_es_internal_cfg.h L862-879; sample_defs example_platform_cfg.h L856). On timeout ES only writes a syslog line and continues (cfe_es_start.c L204-229).

(b) CFE_ES_WaitForSystemState runs under the ES lock first. If the caller has an app record, it raises the caller's own AppState when that state is lower. For non-core apps the mapping is OPERATIONAL→RUNNING, APPS_INIT→LATE_INIT and SHUTDOWN→STOPPED. For core apps, any state at or above CORE_READY maps to RUNNING. It then polls SystemState without the lock and returns CFE_ES_OPERATION_TIMED_OUT if the timeout expires. A successful return only means SystemState reached the requested state, which ES may have entered after its own sync timed out. There is no infinite-wait option. CFE_ES_RunLoop is the only other routine that raises AppState to RUNNING (cfe_es_api.c L469-472).

(c) CFE_ES_WaitForStartupSync is a void wrapper that discards the status (L616-619). The header says values below 1000 are rounded up (cfe_es.h L440-444), but no rounding is implemented. At cFE 546a0025, core-service startup is serialized, and the specific cFE #73 crash path is closed in the code. In #73, TIME runs first because of its priority, calls CFE_SB_CreatePipe with an uninitialized SB AppId of 0 (then a valid ID), goes through EVS_NotRegistered and EVS_SendEvent, and EVS_IsFiltered is reached with an unchecked EVS_AppID of 0xFFFFFFFF. Three separate changes break that chain at this commit. This is an inference from reading the code plus 24 pc-linux native runs; no other platform was tested.

(1) Serialized startup. CFE_ES_CreateObjects (cfe_es_start.c L767-876, called from CFE_ES_Main L189) first calls EarlyInit for every CoreObjectTable entry. That happens before any core-app task is created. It is not "before any task exists": the root thread and the PSP soft_timebase 'cFS-Master' thread already exist. It then creates core-app tasks one at a time in MISSION_CORE_MODULES order. Only es, evs, sb, tbl and time have a TaskMain; config and fs have EarlyInit only, and msg, sbr and resourceid have neither. After each task is created it calls CFE_ES_MainTaskSyncDelay(CFE_ES_AppState_RUNNING, CFE_PLATFORM_CORE_MAX_STARTUP_MSEC) at L861. That function polls every 50 ms until every registered app is at least RUNNING. The timeout's default value is 30000 ms and is configurable. On failure or timeout the code panics (CFE_PSP_Panic, L871).

(2) EVS_SendEvent guards EVS_AppID (cfe_evs_utils.c L613-623). It uses EVS_GetAppDataByID, which checks the index, and EVS_AppDataIsMatch, which checks for NULL and for a matching ID.

(3) AppID 0 is now CFE_RESOURCEID_UNDEFINED. CFE_ResourceId_ToIndex rejects it, so CFE_EVS_SendEventWithAppID returns CFE_EVS_APP_ILLEGAL_APP_ID (cfe_evs.c L185-188) and never reaches EVS_NotRegistered.

Runtime probes (cFE 546a0025, OSAL 5befd8e9, PSP 36c24cb9, SIMULATION=native) logged the 'Initialized' events in the order ES, EVS, SB, TBL, TIME in all 4 configurations and all 24 runs (4 primary runs plus 5 repeats per configuration). The configurations were SCHED_RR on all CPUs, SCHED_RR pinned to cpu0, SCHED_OTHER on all CPUs, and SCHED_OTHER on cpu0. In the RR runs, CFE_TIME has the highest RT priority of the five core main tasks (75, against ES 72, EVS 74, SB 73, TBL 71). This follows from CFE_PLATFORM_TIME_START_TASK_PRIORITY=60, the lowest priority number. TIME's child tasks run at 88.

A residual issue remains. On every successful pipe creation (Status==CFE_SUCCESS), CFE_SB_CreatePipe sends a debug event with CFE_EVS_SendEventWithAppID(..., CFE_SB_Global.AppId, ...) at cfe_sb_api.c L272-281. I re-read every cited source at the pinned commit. I checked the local clone against GitHub raw files and they matched byte-for-byte. I also read issues #2663 and #73 and the local probe logs.

The claim's substance holds:
- CreateObjects runs EarlyInit for every core module first.
- It then creates core tasks one at a time and blocks each in MainTaskSyncDelay(RUNNING, 30000) at L861, panicking on timeout.
- EVS_SendEvent validates EVS_AppID.
- CreatePipe sends a debug event via SendEventWithAppID with CFE_SB_Global.AppId at L272-281 and ignores the result.
- #2663 is open, dated 2025-08-06, and reports CFE_EVS_APP_ILLEGAL_APP_ID being silently ignored during ES/EVS init.

Five points of wording are imprecise, none fatal:
(a) 'Before any task exists' is too strong. The root thread and the PSP 'cFS-Master' timebase thread already exist; what is true is that no core-app task exists yet.
(b) The parenthetical list includes fs (and the full list also has config), but neither has a TaskMain. Tasks are created only for es, evs, sb, tbl and time.
(c) 'Unconditionally' is wrong. The debug event is gated on Status==CFE_SUCCESS; what it lacks is any check of SB's registration with EVS.
(d) '#73 cannot be reproduced' is an inference. It rests on three code changes (serialization, the EVS_SendEvent guard, and AppID 0 now being undefined) plus 24 pc-linux native runs, not on proof.
(e) #2663 also names CFE_SB_Subscribe, and its reporter environment says 'cFE v6.7'.

I also confirmed statically that the #2663 mechanism is present at the pinned commit. SB's AppId is zeroed in EarlyInit and set only in SB's own TaskInit. ES and EVS create pipes before the SB task exists. AppId 0 fails ToIndex, so the call returns ILLEGAL_APP_ID. This was not checked at runtime, which agrees with the claim's 'not reproduced'.

CFE_ES_CreateObjects (cfe_es_start.c L767-876), running in the ES startup thread, first calls EarlyInit for every core-module object-table entry that has one: CONFIG, ES, EVS, FS, SB, TBL, TIME. Only then does it create any core-app task. msg, sbr and resourceid have no EarlyInit, and OS/PSP threads already exist at this point. It then creates the core-app tasks one at a time: ES, EVS, SB, TBL, TIME. FS has no task. This order comes from the default MISSION_CORE_MODULES list, which missions may change. After each task is created, the startup thread polls until every used app record reaches RUNNING, within CFE_PLATFORM_CORE_MAX_STARTUP_MSEC (default 30000; L861). If that times out, it calls CFE_PSP_Panic (L864-871). A core app reaches RUNNING only when it calls CFE_ES_WaitForSystemState(CORE_READY) after its TaskInit. That wait then blocks it until ES sets CORE_READY. Child tasks created during TaskInit (ES_BG_TASK, the TIME tone and 1Hz tasks) run concurrently. The #73 crash sequence is therefore not reachable in this code under the default core-module configuration. This is an inference from reading the code, not a failed reproduction attempt. scope.reasoning:
The substance of C12 holds when checked against primary code at the pinned commit. Core-app TaskInit is serialized by CreateObjects plus MainTaskSyncDelay plus each core app's WaitForSystemState(CORE_READY), regardless of priority. The panic on timeout is real. Both EVS entry points validate AppIDs before indexing, so every ingredient of the #73 segfault is blocked. The #2663 residual is real and visible in the code: CFE_SB_Global.AppId stays 0 until SB TaskInit, while ES and EVS create pipes earlier, and the return value is dropped. Issue metadata (open, 2025-08-06) matches. I therefore do not refute it.

Under the overreach lens, though, several phrasings claim more than the evidence supports:
(1) "cannot be reproduced" is stated as fact. It is an inference from code reading plus non-occurrence in 24 Linux runs. No targeted reproduction or fault injection was done, and the source ledger itself labels it as interpretation.
(2) "in every configuration" means the 4 probed configurations on one platform: Linux native debug builds with default priorities. In two of them, without CAP_SYS_NICE, core tasks had no RT priority at all.
(3) "before any task exists" is literally false. The ES startup thread, which runs CreateObjects, and the OSAL/PSP threads exist. The correct statement is "before any core-app task is created".
(4) Listing "fs" among the tasks is wrong: FS and CONFIG have EarlyInit only. The order is the default MISSION_CORE_MODULES, which missions may reorder.
(5) "unconditionally" is wrong: the debug event is sent only when Status == CFE_SUCCESS. The accurate point is that there is no init-state guard.
(6) "=30000" is a default platform value.
(7) MainTaskSyncDelay waits until all registered apps reach RUNNING, not "each" one.

Each of these can be fixed by narrower wording without changing the conclusion, so refuted=false and the corrected claim carries the precise scope. Sources I could not open: the GitHub API and MCP for nasa/cFE were blocked. The issue pages were read via WebFetch of the HTML.

counter.corrected_claim: At cFE 546a0025 (head of the dev branch; main at 12cb84f has the same structure), the main tasks of the core services start one at a time, so the cFE #73 crash path is closed. Two independent things close it. CFE_ES_CreateObjects runs EarlyInit for every core-object-table entry (CFE_CONFIG, ES, EVS, FS, SB, TBL, TIME, plus MSG/SBR/RESOURCEID entries that have no hooks) before any core-app task is created. PSP/OSAL threads such as the soft timebase already exist at that point. It then creates the main tasks of the entries that have a TaskMain (ES, EVS, SB, TBL, TIME; FS has none), one at a time, in the default MISSION_CORE_MODULES order, which a mission can change. After each one it calls CFE_ES_MainTaskSyncDelay(RUNNING, CFE_PLATFORM_CORE_MAX_STARTUP_MSEC; default 30000) at cfe_es_start.c:861. That call waits until every used app record is RUNNING and panics on timeout. A core task sets itself to RUNNING inside CFE_ES_WaitForSystemState after its TaskInit returns, whether or not TaskInit succeeded. So the TaskInit calls are serialized, but child tasks (ES_BG_TASK, the TIME tone/1Hz tasks) run at the same time as later initialization. Separately, CFE_EVS_SendEventWithAppID (cfe_evs.c:185-189) and EVS_SendEvent (cfe_evs_utils.c:617-623) range-check the AppId through EVS_GetAppDataByID before any table lookup. In 24 probe runs over 4 scheduling configurations (RR, where CFE_TIME has the highest rtprio of the core main tasks at 75, and no-cap; all CPUs and CPU0 only), ES, EVS, SB, TBL and TIME initialized in that order every time. 'Not reproducible' is an inference from the code plus these runs, not a targeted reproduction attempt. On every successful call, with no check of SB's own init state, CFE_SB_CreatePipe sends a debug event with CFE_SB_Global.AppId (cfe_sb_api.c L272-281) and discards the return value. Subscribe and the TransmitMsg no-subscriber path do the same. CFE_SB_Global.AppId stays 0 (memset in CFE_SB_EarlyInit) until SB's TaskInit sets it (cfe_sb_task.c:128). So during ES/EVS TaskInit, EVS_GetAppDataByID(0) returns NULL and the call returns CFE_EVS_APP_ILLEGAL_APP_ID, which nothing checks. This is open issue cFE #2663 (2025-08-06). The behavior is no longer unreproduced: a gdb run of the pinned native build reproduced it 24 times during ES and EVS init (2 pipe-created, 4 subscription-received, 18 send-no-subscribers events). scope.corrected_claim: At cFE 546a0025, when the owner is still registered and the table's registry record has no active buffer (CFE_TBL_RegRecIsTableLoaded false, i.e. no Load/activation yet), CFE_TBL_GetAddress and CFE_TBL_GetAddresses return CFE_TBL_ERR_NEVER_LOADED (0xcc000005) with *TblPtr = NULL and do not set the access descriptor's LockFlag (cfe_tbl_registry.c L192-196; the only LockFlag=true write in modules/tbl/fsw/src is L207, on the loaded path; cfe_tbl_api.c L450 pre-sets NULL). An unowned table returns CFE_TBL_ERR_UNREGISTERED first. "Never loaded" here is TBL's internal notion. Two kinds of table get an active buffer without an explicit CFE_TBL_Load, so for them GetAddress succeeds and locks: dump-only tables with an internal buffer (activated at registration, cfe_tbl_regrec.c L375-386) and critical tables restored from CDS (cfe_tbl_internal.c L1010). In the never-loaded case, CFE_TBL_ReleaseAddress also returns NEVER_LOADED (cfe_tbl_api.c L492 -> cfe_tbl_transaction.c L303-306) and unconditionally clears LockFlag (api.c L489), which has no effect here. The header (cfe_tbl.h L540-544, and the same note for GetAddresses at L620-624; blob f3510424 = revision S10) says the call 'will still return a valid table pointer to a table with all zero content' that must be released. Revision note §7.1 line 317 states this as [확인된 사실] (confirmed fact) citing only S10, so for this commit it is a doc-vs-implementation mismatch. In v6.7.0 (tag 2105b93), GetAddressInternal set LockFlag and returned the active-buffer pointer before GetNextNotification returned NEVER_LOADED (cfe_tbl_internal.c L571, L578, L616-619), and Register zeroed internal buffers (cfe_tbl_api.c L272). So v6.7.0 matched the header for tables with internal buffers, but not for user-defined-address tables, whose buffer pointer was NULL until loaded (api.c L278). A runtime probe gave the same result in 4 configurations: owner app, default single-buffered table, ptr pre-set to 0x1. The configurations were scheduling variants (SCHED_RR with or without CAP_SYS_NICE, all CPUs or cpu0) of one native-Linux debug build of cFE 546a0025, OSAL 5befd8e and PSP 36c24cb. It printed 'GetAddress(T) BEFORE load st=0xcc000005 ptr=(nil)' and 'ReleaseAddress(T) BEFORE load st=0xcc000005'. The probe did not observe LockFlag directly; that part rests on the source code.

I checked each sub-claim myself against the pinned source, the v6.7.0 tag, the revision note and the local probe logs. Everything stated is accurate for its stated scope. The claim is pinned to one commit and one historical tag, and it does not generalize to other versions or platforms, so I do not refute it.

It is imprecise in three places where it is broader than the evidence:
1. "A table that has never been loaded" really means "the TBL registry has no active buffer." Two kinds of table get an active buffer without CFE_TBL_Load, so for them GetAddress succeeds and sets LockFlag: dump-only internal-buffer tables (at registration) and CDS-restored critical tables. An unowned table returns UNREGISTERED first. This matters for the TBL API model and for the 'release after NEVER_LOADED' benchmark row.
2. "In v6.7.0 the implementation matched the header" holds only for internal-buffer tables. Those buffers were zeroed at registration. For user-defined-address tables in v6.7.0, the returned pointer would be NULL, not a pointer to valid zero content.
3. The "4 configurations" are scheduling and CPU-affinity variants of a single native-Linux debug build, run on one default single-buffered table from the owner app. The probe recorded status and pointer only. The "LockFlag not set" part is therefore supported by the code alone, not observed at runtime.

The claim also leaves out that GetAddresses behaves the same way (header L620-624, api.c L543). The core correction stands. Revision §7.1 L317 presents the header's text as a confirmed fact, but at 546a0025 the implementation returns a NULL pointer and takes no lock, so it does not match that text.

recheck.corrected_claim:
At cFE 546a0025, table locking is per access descriptor, not per pointer. A descriptor is one per table handle, and it carries the AppId and HandleId. Each descriptor holds one LockFlag and one BufferIndex.

- **GetAddress:** CFE_TBL_TxnGetTableAddress sets LockFlag=true and records the ID of the current active buffer. It does not check whether the descriptor is already locked.
- **ReleaseAddress:** it changes only LockFlag (sets it false). BufferIndex is left as it was. The notification lookup it also does is read-only.
- **Consequence:** a second GetAddress without a release moves the protection to the then-active buffer.

At runtime this happened in all 4 probe runs (R1-R4). A sharer took a pointer to double-buffered table D, which read 1. It then called GetAddress(D) a second time without releasing (the second pointer read 2). After the owner's Load(D,v3), the never-released first pointer read 3.

Update behaviour depends on buffering.

- **Single-buffered (CFE_TBL_OPT_DEFAULT):** Load stages the data in a shared load buffer. The activation step (UpdateInternal → GetInactiveBufferExclusive) checks every descriptor of the table for a lock on the table's single buffer. If one is locked, Load returns CFE_TBL_INFO_TABLE_LOCKED (0x4c000018), which is a positive informational code. The load is left in progress. After the address is released, GetStatus reports UPDATE_PENDING (0x4c000004). The owner's Manage, or Update, then applies the load and Manage returns INFO_UPDATED (0x4c00000e).
  - This was observed with the owner's own descriptor holding the lock, in the probe and in the cFE functional test. The functional test's own comment says the Manage call "shouldn't be necessary".
  - The case where a sharer holds the lock follows from the same descriptor scan. That is inference from the code and was not run.
- **Double-buffered:** Load writes the inactive buffer and makes it active. A sharer that holds the previously active buffer keeps seeing the old content (val 1 at t+3s).
  - **When the next load is refused:** only while the holder's descriptor still points at the now-inactive buffer. In that case it fails in ValidateLoadRequest/GetWorkingBuffer with CFE_TBL_ERR_NO_BUFFER_AVAIL (0xcc00000f). No load is left in progress: GetStatus returns 0, and a load after the release succeeds.
  - **If the holder re-acquires without releasing:** as with D, the protection moves and the next load overwrites the buffer behind the old pointer.

recheck.reasoning:
I re-opened every cited code range at the pinned commit. The local clone is clean and byte-identical to the GitHub raw files at the SHA. I also re-read the local probe summary and the probe source to confirm what was actually run.

**Per-descriptor model.** All parts of it are directly supported by the code:
- The descriptor holds one LockFlag and one BufferIndex.
- GetAddress sets LockFlag and records the active buffer ID without checking an existing lock.
- ReleaseAddress writes only LockFlag.
- The lock check matches descriptors by buffer and LockFlag.

The runtime observation is real and reproduced in all four runs: the first D pointer, never released, read 3 after Load(v3) because the second GetAddress had moved the lock. The status codes match cfe_error.h.

**Imprecisions:**
1. **Single-buffered evidence covers only the owner's own lock.** The probe and the cFE functional test both lock with the owner's own descriptor. 'A load while a descriptor holds the buffer' held by a sharer is inferred from the shared descriptor scan; it was not executed.
2. **The completion step can be Manage or Update.** The pending load can be completed by the owner's Manage or by Update. The 0x4c000018 is a positive INFO return from Load, not an error. Upstream's own test comment calls the need for Manage something that 'shouldn't be necessary', so this behaviour may change.
3. **The NO_BUFFER_AVAIL refusal is conditional.** In the double-buffered case it happens only while the holder's descriptor still points at the now-inactive buffer. If the holder re-acquires without releasing, the next load succeeds and overwrites the old pointer's buffer, which is the D case.
4. **'Proceeds while a sharer holds the old buffer'.** When the load starts, the sharer holds the then-active buffer; it becomes the old buffer only after activation.

None of these contradict the claim; they narrow it. So refuted=false, with a corrected, more precise statement.

At cFE 546a0025 (tip of the dev branch; the locking code is unchanged from v7.0.1, and v6.7.0 behaves the same way in substance), table locking is per access descriptor (one per handle, carrying the AppId), not per pointer. Each descriptor holds a single (LockFlag, BufferIndex) pair. On its success path, where the table is owned and loaded, CFE_TBL_GetAddress sets LockFlag and records the ID of the buffer that is active at that moment. It does not lock when it returns ERR_NEVER_LOADED or ERR_UNREGISTERED. ReleaseAddress clears only LockFlag and leaves BufferIndex and the Updated flag alone. A second GetAddress without a release therefore overwrites BufferIndex and moves protection to the new active buffer. Single-buffered tables: when the owner calls CFE_TBL_Load while any descriptor (the owner's own included) holds the table's buffer locked, the data is loaded into a shared working buffer and validated, but activation in UpdateInternal is refused. Load returns CFE_TBL_INFO_TABLE_LOCKED (0x4c000018). The load stays in progress: GetStatus returns UPDATE_PENDING (0x4c000004), and any new Load is rejected with ERR_LOAD_IN_PROGRESS. It completes only after the address is released and the owner calls Manage, which returns INFO_UPDATED (0x4c00000e), or calls Update, which returns CFE_SUCCESS. On the ground-command path (LOAD_CC then ACTIVATE_CC) the load command itself does not return TABLE_LOCKED; the owner's Manage/Update reports it.

Double-buffered tables: the lock is checked only when the inactive buffer is reserved at load start. A load while a holder locks the currently active buffer goes ahead and switches the active buffer, and the holder keeps seeing the old content. The next load, whose target is the still-locked old buffer, is refused at request validation with CFE_TBL_ERR_NO_BUFFER_AVAIL (0xcc00000f), and no load is left in progress. The official header and developer-guide wording that table updates cannot occur while addresses are unreleased is therefore inaccurate for double-buffered tables.

scope.corrected_claim:
At cFE 546a0025, table locking is tracked per access descriptor (one per table handle). Each Register or Share call allocates its own descriptor, so one app can hold several handles to the same table. Nothing tracks individual pointers. Each descriptor holds one LockFlag, one Updated flag and one BufferIndex. A successful GetAddress unconditionally sets LockFlag=true and overwrites BufferIndex with the current active buffer. ReleaseAddress clears only LockFlag; it leaves BufferIndex and Updated alone and just reports the notification status. So a second GetAddress without a release moves protection to the new active buffer.

The lock check is buffer-identity based: any descriptor of that table with LockFlag set whose BufferIndex points to the buffer counts. Where the check happens depends on the buffering option:
- **Double-buffered:** the check runs at load time, when the load acquires the inactive buffer (PrepareNewLoadBuff → GetInactiveBufferExclusive). The update then just flips the active buffer.
- **Single-buffered:** data is loaded into a shared working buffer, and the check runs at update time, when that data is copied into the table's only buffer (UpdateInternal).

Observed on a native-Linux (SIMULATION=native) build, consistent across 4 probe runs:
- **Single-buffered T, owner's own CFE_TBL_Load:** with the owner's own descriptor holding T, Load returned CFE_TBL_INFO_TABLE_LOCKED (0x4c000018) and the update stayed pending (GetStatus = 0x4c000004). It completed only after ReleaseAddress plus a later Manage, which returned INFO_UPDATED (0x4c00000e). The cFE functional test asserts the same and comments that the extra Manage "shouldn't be necessary". A sharer's descriptor should block the same way, but that is inferred from the code (the check iterates all descriptors); it was not run. Calling CFE_TBL_Update should also complete the pending update (code inference).
- **Double-buffered, owner's API Load while a sharer holds the active buffer:** the load succeeds, and the sharer's pointer keeps showing old content (v1). What happens next depends on the sharer:
  - If the sharer neither releases nor calls GetAddress again (table E), the next Load fails with CFE_TBL_ERR_NO_BUFFER_AVAIL (0xcc00000f) and nothing is left pending (GetStatus = 0).

scope.reasoning:
I checked every code statement against a local clone of nasa/cFE at the pinned commit, and the cited permalink line ranges match the code. The mechanism holds:
- Each descriptor has a single LockFlag/BufferIndex pair.
- GetAddress overwrites both unconditionally.
- ReleaseAddress only clears LockFlag.
- The lock check is a scan over all of the table's descriptors, keyed on which buffer each one points to.

The runtime values (3 instead of 1, 0x4c000018, 0x4c000004 then 0x4c00000e, 0xcc00000f with GetStatus=0) are reproduced in all 4 full probe runs. So the core claim is right, and I do not refute it.

It does state some parts more broadly than the evidence:
1. **"A load ... returns TABLE_LOCKED" covers only one path.** It is true for the owner's CFE_TBL_Load API, because LoadFinish calls UpdateInternal right away. In the Table Services ground Load+Activate path, the code suggests the load command does not return TABLE_LOCKED; the lock surfaces later at the owner's Manage/Update. That path was not run.
2. **The single-buffered lock was observed only for self-locking.** Both the probe (T lines) and the cFE functional test have the owner holding its own address. That a sharer's held pointer blocks the same way is a code inference (CheckInactiveBufferHelper iterates all descriptors), not a runtime result.
3. **"Per handle and AppId" is imprecise.** Each Share call allocates a new descriptor, so the unit is the handle/descriptor, and one app can have several.
4. **The double-buffered refusal is conditional.** It happens only while the holder's descriptor still has LockFlag set and points at the inactive buffer. The D case shows that a re-GetAddress removes that protection, and the next load then overwrites the buffer behind the stale pointer.
5. **"Pending until Manage" is one exit, not the only one.** A direct Update should also complete it (code inference). The test comment "This call shouldn't be necessary" shows the maintainers regard this as a quirk, so it may change in later versions.
6. **The runtime evidence is narrow.** It is a native-Linux simulation build with 4 full runs; the 20 repeat runs only reproduced the T part.

The claim's evidence also misses the most direct source for the per-buffering split, PrepareNewLoadBuff (cfe_tbl_loadbuff.c:434-458). The cited loadbuff.c L146-189 (LocateLoadBufferByID) is only supporting detail.
