recheck.corrected_claim:
At cFE 546a0025, restarting an app is an asynchronous request that is torn down later. CFE_ES_RestartApp, ReloadApp and DeleteApp (cfe_es_api.c L165-284, not the cited appctrl.c range) run no teardown. They record the request in ControlReq.AppControlRequest under the ES lock, with two extra steps: RestartApp first checks with OS_stat that the app file exists and returns CFE_ES_FILE_IO_ERR if not, and ReloadApp also overwrites StartParams.BasicInfo.FileName. The ES background scan (CFE_ES_RunAppTableScan) then moves the app to WAITING and starts a timer of KILL_TIMEOUT*SCAN_RATE; the app normally leaves RunLoop and calls ExitApp, which sets it to STOPPED. When the timer runs out, the scan calls CFE_ES_ProcessControlRequest. That function calls CFE_ES_CleanUpApp and, for restart or reload, CFE_ES_AppCreate, which gives the app a new AppId. CleanUpApp calls the core-module AppCleanupCb callbacks (EVS, SB, TA, TBL, TIME) before deleting the app's tasks, pools and module.
- **SB:** CFE_SB_CleanUpApp deletes every pipe the app owns. It removes the pipe from all routes, drains and discards the queued buffers, deletes the OS queue and releases the app's zero-copy buffers.
- **TBL:** CFE_TBL_CleanUpApp drops the app's pending dump requests and releases all of its access descriptors. Tables the app owned are marked un-owned (OwnerAppId=UNDEFINED). Their registry record is freed only once no access descriptor remains.
- **EVS:** CFE_EVS_CleanUpApp frees the app's EVS record.
- **Routes:** SBR has no function that removes a route; only CFE_SBR_Init clears them. So routes and their sequence counters survive the cleanup. This comes from the code having no removal path, not from a runtime check across a restart.
If the restarted app owned a table that another app still shares, the new instance's CFE_TBL_Register returns CFE_TBL_ERR_DUPLICATE_NOT_OWNED (0xcc00000d) until every sharer has released its descriptor (in the probe, the single sharer's Unregister). After CleanUpApp the sharer's GetAddress returns CFE_TBL_ERR_UNREGISTERED (0xcc000009) with a NULL pointer. Before cleanup, the sharer's GetAddress still returned the old valid pointer for about 1.5 s, even after the old instance had called ExitApp. This was seen in 1 run of each of the 4 native-Linux probe configurations (R1-R4). The time from the RestartApp call to the new instance's entry was 1.57-1.63 s, and the AppId went from 1114121 to 1114123 (0x11000b). After the sharer unregistered, Register succeeded.

Restart, reload and delete are asynchronous. ProcessControlRequest runs CleanUpApp and then AppCreate with a new AppId, and the cleanup callbacks run before the tasks are deleted. 5. "Routes persist" rests on the code having no removal path, not on a runtime check across a restart. The reproduction is one run per configuration on native Linux. The retry and unregister timing comes from the probe's design.

The EVS cleanup and SBR facts are correct but are not in the claim's cited evidence list.

scope.corrected_claim: At cFE 546a0025 (source reading), restart is an asynchronous request followed by teardown. Later, the ES background scan moves a RUNNING app with a pending request to WAITING, with a kill timer of APP_KILL_TIMEOUT x APP_SCAN_RATE (5 x 1000 ms in the sample config). SB deletes every pipe the app owns: it removes the pipe from all routes, drains and discards the queued messages and deletes the OS queue; it also releases the app's zero-copy buffers. TBL drops dump requests for tables the app owns and releases all of the app's access descriptors. It marks tables the app owned as un-owned (OwnerAppId = UNDEFINED). Such a registry record is freed only when no access descriptors remain. EVS frees the app's EVS registration, and TIME clears its synch callback. SBR has no route-removal function, so routes and their sequence counters persist; this part is source-only and was not exercised in a restart run. This lasts until every remaining access descriptor is released, by Unregister or by the sharer's own cleanup. Once cleanup has run, the sharer's GetAddress returns CFE_TBL_ERR_UNREGISTERED (0xcc000009) with a NULL pointer. Between the RestartApp call and cleanup (about 1.5 s here), the sharer still got the old buffer with status 0x4c00000e or 0. The TBL/ES part was observed once in each of the 4 probe configurations. All four are scheduling variants on one native Linux build with OSAL permissive mode: SCHED_RR with CAP_SYS_NICE or default TS, all CPUs or CPU0. In each run there was one sharer, and the owner exited cooperatively from a 500 ms RunLoop poll. counter.corrected_claim: At cFE 546a0025, restarting an app is an asynchronous request followed by teardown. CFE_ES_RestartApp, ReloadApp and DeleteApp only check and record the request. They accept only an external app in the RUNNING state, and Restart/Reload return CFE_ES_FILE_IO_ERR if the app file is missing. Reload also copies the new filename. Then they set ControlReq.AppControlRequest. The ES background scan, CFE_ES_RunAppTableScan, later calls CFE_ES_ProcessControlRequest. That runs CFE_ES_CleanUpApp and then, for restart or reload, CFE_ES_AppCreate, which gives a new AppId. CleanUpApp invokes every core module's AppCleanupCb before it deletes the app's tasks and pools. Those callbacks are SB, TBL, EVS, TIME and a placeholder for TA. SB deletes every pipe the app owns: it removes the pipe from all routes, drains queued buffers and deletes the OS queue. It also releases the app's zero-copy buffers. TBL cancels dump requests for tables the app owns and releases all of the app's access descriptors. It also marks the app's owned tables as unowned (OwnerAppId=UNDEFINED). The registry record keeps its name and buffers until its last access link is removed. EVS frees the app's registration and TIME clears its synch callback. SB routes and their sequence counters persist, because SBR has no route-removal function. In this version (code introduced by the v7.0.0 'cFS Draco' commit c1ab1b7; all earlier tags cleared the table name), a problem follows when the restarted app owned a table that another app shares. The new instance's CFE_TBL_Register returns CFE_TBL_ERR_DUPLICATE_NOT_OWNED (0xcc00000d) until every remaining access descriptor is released (each sharer's Unregister, or the sharer's own cleanup). After cleanup, but not before, the sharer's GetAddress returns CFE_TBL_ERR_UNREGISTERED (0xcc000009) with a NULL pointer. Between RestartApp and cleanup the sharer still gets the old pointer. The official TBL FAQ (docs/src/cfe_tbl.dox L333-339) still describes the older behavior and does not match the code. One probe scenario reproduced this in all 4 scheduling configurations. Those are SCHED_RR with or without CAP_SYS_NICE and all CPUs or CPU0 only, one run each on one host, with the sharer app calling CFE_ES_RestartApp. Time from the RestartApp call to the new app's entry was 1.57-1.63 s, and AppId went from 1114121 (0x110009) to 1114123 (0x11000b). That latency comes from the ES scan schedule with this configuration (APP_SCAN_RATE 1000 ms, KILL_TIMEOUT 5), not from cFE in general.

counter.reasoning:
I checked every mechanical step of the claim against the pinned source (a clean local clone at 546a0025) and against the raw probe logs. The steps are: the asynchronous request; the background scan calling ProcessControlRequest, which runs CleanUpApp and then AppCreate; core-module cleanup callbacks running before tasks are deleted; SB pipe deletion (remove from routes, drain the queue, delete the OS queue); TBL releasing access descriptors; EVS freeing the app's registration; routes and sequence counters persisting (SBR has no route-removal API); DUPLICATE_NOT_OWNED on Register; UNREGISTERED with a NULL pointer on GetAddress; and reproduction in all 4 configurations with AppId 1114121 to 1114123 and about 1.6 s. All of these hold, so the claim is not refuted.

Searching for counter-evidence turned up one substantive limit and several imprecisions.

(1) The DUPLICATE_NOT_OWNED dependency depends on the version. Every cFE version before the v7.0.0 'cFS Draco' squash commit c1ab1b7 (2026-01-22) cleared the table name during app cleanup and Unregister. That includes v6.7.0, v6.8.0, v7.0.0-rc1, draco-rc5 and dev at fcbb179 from 2025-12-17. In those versions the restarted owner's Register would not hit the unowned 'shadow' record; this is an inference from source and was not run. The official TBL FAQ at the same commit still describes that older behavior, so the docs and the code disagree. For the research note this means the behavior must not be generalized to cFS or to deployed missions. A benchmark or analyzer rule built on it must pin cFE 7.0.x or later, and the doc/code mismatch is itself worth reporting.

(2) The cleanup list is incomplete:
- TIME and TA callbacks also run.
- SB also releases zero-copy buffers.
- TBL also cancels dump requests and marks owned tables unowned while keeping their records.

(3) 'Until the sharer calls Unregister' should read: until all remaining access links are released. That can happen through any sharer's Unregister or through the sharer's own app cleanup.

(4) UNREGISTERED starts only after CleanUpApp runs. Between the RestartApp call and cleanup, the sharer still got valid pointers (R1 L148-150).

(5) The request APIs also validate before setting ControlReq: core apps and apps that are not RUNNING are rejected, and Restart/Reload check that the file exists.

(6) The 1.6 s figure and the 4-configuration replication come from a single probe scenario on one host, one run per config, with configurations differing only in scheduling class and CPU affinity. The latency follows the ES scan schedule and its configuration (APP_SCAN_RATE, KILL_TIMEOUT 5 × 1000 ms for an app that does not exit), so it is not a general cFE property.

I found no GitHub issue reporting the re-registration change; nasa/cFE #1509 is a related open issue about table-sharing races. I read the source directly and did not depend on fetches from blocked sites.

I re-checked every sub-claim against code at the pinned SHAs, confirmed those files byte-for-byte against GitHub raw, and checked the local run logs. The substance holds.

One imprecision: the 'missing-data event' is DEBUG type, and the default EVS type flag of 0xE turns DEBUG off, so the observable freshness signal by default is MissingDataCtr in HK telemetry.

However, the quotation is not verbatim: the source says 'Defer subscribing until the system is operational will avoid possibly seeing...'. Also, 'subscribes only after' overgeneralizes: TO_LAB subscribes to its own command MIDs with literal arguments in TO_LAB_init, before the sync. Only the table-driven telemetry subscriptions are deferred, and the sync has a 10 s default timeout.

(c) The behavior is correct: SCH_LAB builds headers from table MessageIDs at lines 246-248 and transmits them at line 131. But the cited sch_lab repo table is an empty default with its example entries commented out. The populated table actually built is the bundle's sample_defs/tables/sch_lab_table.c.

(d) The 8 successful runs each show exactly 4 lines before OPERATIONAL, and 0x808 is CFE_EVS_LONG_EVENT_MSG_MID. However, these lines were logged by CFE_SB (EID 14) naming the four apps as senders; the four apps did not log them. The cap of 4 is confirmed as CFE_EVS_FIRST_4_STOP on CFE_SB_SEND_NO_SUBS_EID. That filter covers no-subscriber events for all MIDs, so the 'true count unknown' conclusion is a sound inference. SB's NoSubscribersCounter would hold the count but was not captured.

The opening statement ('much of' the graph is data- or config-driven) is a qualitative interpretation that was not measured. Because the default table MIDs are compile-time macros, the default table images can be resolved statically from source plus build config; what is dynamic is reloading tables and ground commands (inference).

None of these points reverses the claim, so refuted=false with a corrected wording.

counter.reasoning:
I checked every line reference against the pinned, clean checkout. These SHAs are also today's upstream dev HEADs, so no later fix changes the behavior. HK and to_lab main (May 2026) keep the same logic. The core claim holds: HK, TO_LAB and SCH_LAB take MIDs from tables, TO_LAB also from a ground command, and the 8 logs show exactly 4 capped no-subscriber events. No counter-evidence refutes it, but several parts are imprecise or under-scoped.

(1) The HK missing-data event is DEBUG type. Under the default EVS type mask 0xE an operator would not see it; the MissingDataCtr counter is the observable signal. In the bundle, nothing sends HK's combined-packet request, so the freshness path is not exercised at run time.

(2) TO_LAB defers only its table-driven telemetry subscriptions, not its command MIDs, and only until OPERATIONAL or a 10 s timeout. The quoted comment is slightly misquoted ('to avoid' vs 'will avoid'). The deferral is recent (April 2026, in v7.0.1 only), so older releases behave differently. A checker built on older code must not assume it.

(3) The sch_lab table cited for (c) is the empty upstream default. The run-time MIDs come from the bundle override sample_defs/tables/sch_lab_table.c, which I confirmed from the build's DependInfo. This supports the claim's thesis that build configuration selects the table, but the cited evidence file is the wrong one. SCH_LAB also never re-reads its table after init.

(4) The 'No subscribers' lines are emitted by CFE_SB naming the senders, not logged by those apps. The cap is CFE_EVS_FIRST_4_STOP on that EID, shared across all MsgIds. The true count is unknown only from the console; SB's HK NoSubscribersCounter tracks it. A 9th run (run_root.log) failed early and is excluded.

Interpretive caution for the why_central use: three of the four events occur before CORE_READY, before any app is loaded. DS and HS also subscribe to 0x808 during their own init. So these log lines are not evidence specifically of 'TO_LAB's intended first-message loss'. Only the TO_LAB-sender event plausibly follows from the d3d52da deferral; that is an inference from the diff, which removed the subscription from before the init-event code.

Also, 'much of the graph' holds by run-time edge count (inference from table sizes). It does not hold by call-site count: about 8 of 47 sites take a MID from data.

Not verified: whether HS event monitoring is enabled in this bundle's HS config, and exact subscription timing relative to the SAMPLE_APP and LC events.

scope.reasoning:
The core thesis holds and every cited line exists and says roughly what the claim says, so I do not refute it. Several sub-claims are stated more broadly than the evidence supports, or are misattributed:

(1) In (b), 'It deliberately subscribes only after CFE_ES_WaitForStartupSync' overgeneralizes. Only the table-driven telemetry subscriptions on Tlm_pipe are deferred. The command MIDs are subscribed in TO_LAB_init before the sync (to_lab_app.c:208, 213). The deferral also belongs to a single 2026-04-21 commit (d3d52da); earlier TO_LAB versions subscribed from the table during init. This is the 'one commit generalized' pattern, so the claim needs version scoping. The wait is bounded by a 10 s timeout, and table updates also re-subscribe (to_lab_app.c:579).

(2) In (d), the text says CFE_SB, CFE_TBL, CFE_TIME and TO_LAB 'logged' the message. In every log line the emitter is CFE_SB (event ID 14, CFE_SB_SEND_NO_SUBS_EID). The four names are the 'sender' field: the apps whose own init events, published as long-event messages on 0x808, had no subscriber. As written the claim misattributes who logged what. '8 native runs' is accurate only as 8 runs that reached OPERATIONAL, all from one build, one config and one host. A 9th log aborted at EVS init. 'True count unknown' holds for the logs only: SB HK NoSubscribersCounter records it but was not captured. It is also my inference that DS (whose filter table includes 0x808) may have subscribed partway through startup, so the number of later unsubscribed sends is unknown for a second reason as well.

(3) In (c), the cited sch_lab repo table at 607e2f9 is empty. The configured MIDs come from the bundle's sample_defs table. SCH_LAB reads its table only once at init and has no update path, so its MIDs are fixed at load time, unlike HK and TO_LAB.

(4) In (a), the missing-data event is DEBUG type, which the default EVS mask 0xE suppresses. The always-on signal is MissingDataCtr. Re-subscription after a table update happens only on the success path.

(5) The headline 'much of the pub/sub graph' rests on three apps. By call site, data- or command-driven subscriptions are a minority: 8 of 47 grep-found sites, spread over HK, TO_LAB, DS, LC, CF and SBN. They are 'much of' the graph only by configured edges (e.g. 37 TO_LAB table entries). The 'literal' MIDs are themselves build-configuration macros.

Scope of my checks: I read the full pinned source files for HK, TO_LAB and SCH_LAB, the relevant cFE SB, EVS and config headers at 546a002, the to_lab commit diff, the bundle's sample_defs tables, and all 9 local run logs. I did not run the system myself. I did not check the DS subscription timing at run time.

Upstream MLIR provides a generic dataflow solver (DataFlowFramework.h) but not the memory model this analysis needs. Experiments with the local mlir-opt built from 1053047a, with the relevant code re-checked on main at ccac700c, showed six things.
(a) LocalAliasAnalysis is the only alias-analysis implementation in upstream mlir/lib. AliasAnalysis.cpp:77 registers it by default. Flang has its own fir::AliasAnalysis, and there is a test-only subclass. It returns MayAlias for two distinct globals reached via llvm.mlir.addressof. The reason is that addressof is ConstantLike, and aliasImpl returns MayAlias for any two constants; a TODO in the code admits this is overly conservative. It returns MustAlias for two different fields of one struct, because llvm.getelementptr implements ViewLikeOpInterface and collectUnderlyingAddressValues unwraps it to its base.
(b) llvm.call does not implement MemoryEffectOpInterface (the interface is named MemoryEffectOpInterface, not MemoryEffectsOpInterface), at both 1053047a and ccac700c. getModRef therefore returns ModRef for every queried location for any llvm.call. This holds even when the call carries an LLVM memory_effects attribute that is all none.
(c) Functions imported from C, including `static` ones that become `llvm.func internal`, get no MLIR sym_visibility. They are therefore public to SymbolOpInterface, and DeadCodeAnalysis (line 192, symbol.isPublic()) marks them as having unknown predecessors.
(d) An indirect call through a `static const` function-pointer table gives the caller only a call-graph edge to <Unknown-Callee-Node>. This holds at both -O0 and -O2.
(e) The upstream test dense analysis (-test-last-modified) returns <unknown> for LLVM-dialect versions of the original note's §44 HandleAttitude→SetState→global.att→Guidance example. This was checked on both a hand-written model and a clang-imported C version, in all three option settings. It also returns <unknown> intraprocedurally when the load goes through a second addressof of the same global.
(f) The DataFlow headers contain no thread, interleaving or concurrency notion. The official DataFlowAnalysis.md tutorial still documents ForwardDataFlowAnalysis and LatticeElement classes that do not exist in the headers at either commit; the current classes are Dense/SparseForwardDataFlowAnalysis, Lattice<T> and getLatticeElement methods.

2. A check that EVS_AppID < CFE_ES_MAX_APPLICATIONS was added, but in the caller EVS_SendEvent. EVS_IsFiltered itself is still unchecked.

The third remedy, consistent AppID values before initialisation, is not visible in the code. EVS_AppID = CFE_EVS_UNDEF_APPID (0xFFFFFFFF) already existed in 6.4.1, so it is the pre-existing sentinel, not a fix. CFE_SB.AppId is still never set before SB's own initialisation in 6.5.0a.

- 32397: Cen X-3, 2022-07-14.

- 43470: spurious Notices after on-board misidentification of 1A 1118-61, 2026-01-20.
- 21077: Cen X-3, 2017-05-08.

**Negative statements I could only partly check.** "Does not say stale or earlier-epoch" and "does not mention attitude or link to 22706" are supported only as far as the snippets go. Full-text absence is unverified.

**Precision issues:**
- 21077 is not the earliest instance. GCN 17919 (2015) and GCN 15695 (2014) also cite the known race. The claim does say only "an earlier instance".
- The arXiv snippet places image production and processing on a separate ADSP21020 DSP. "BAT flight software is C++ on VxWorks on a RAD6000" is therefore a simplification.

**Substantive error.** "So no source links Swift/BAT to cFS" is literally false. Wildermann's 2008 GSFC slides "cFE/CFS" (NTRS 20090005965), which I read in a mirrored text extraction, list "Swift BAT (12/04)" on the slide titled "cFE Heritage". Triana and other pre-cFE GSFC missions appear on the same slide. Search snippets say Cudmore's FSW11 slides show the same heritage list.

**How to read that error.** A heritage listing means BAT's flight software is a pre-cFE ancestor of the cFE design lineage. This fits the BAT Software Bus coming from Triana, which is also listed as heritage. It does not mean BAT runs cFE, which was first used on LRO in 2009 (that date is from snippets only). The claim's central conclusion therefore survives: BAT is not cFS, and it should be cited as a non-cFS example using the "incorrect attitude" wording, with no transfer of mechanism.

**Verdict.** The parts of the claim I could check are supported, apart from the sentence about a cFS link. Because the central conclusion survives, I set refuted=false rather than refuting the whole claim. The corrected_claim must replace "no source links Swift/BAT to cFS" with "no source says BAT runs cFE/cFS; GSFC lists Swift BAT as cFE heritage".

**Caveat on the slide evidence.** The slide comes from a flattened djvu text extraction on a third-party mirror. The heading and the "Swift BAT, 12/04" entry are on the same slide, but the extraction does not preserve the arrow layout. Reading BAT as "heritage" is therefore an inference from the heading text.

scope.reasoning:
Most of the claim's individual facts match what I could check: the dates, trigger numbers and sources of 22706, 32397, 34691, 43470 and 21077, the exact 'incorrect spacecraft attitude information' wording in 22706, and the C++/VxWorks/RAD6000/Triana Software Bus description. Three parts go further than the evidence allows.

(1) The final sentence, 'cFE first flew on LRO (2009) and Swift launched in 2004, so no source links Swift/BAT to cFS', is a negative claim drawn from a date comparison, and it is false as stated. A 2008 GSFC cFE/CFS presentation (NTRS 20090005965) lists 'Swift BAT (12/04)' on its 'cFE Heritage' slide. I confirmed this in the OCR text at a pinned GitHub mirror commit, and two search snippets of the same deck agree. The OCR loses the slide's arrows, so the direction of the relationship cannot be read from the layout. The slide title and the snippets do support 'listed as cFE heritage' (a predecessor), not 'runs cFE'. The date ordering only supports the narrower point that BAT's 2004 flight software was not built on cFE. The two framings also differ in substance: BAT's Triana-heritage CCSDS 'Software Bus' sits in the same GSFC lineage as cFE's Software Bus. Calling BAT 'unrelated to cFS' is therefore also an overreach. It is a cFE-heritage, non-cFS system.

(2) Two absence statements rest on search-engine snippets, because the circular pages were blocked for the claim's author and for me: '22706 does not say stale/earlier-epoch attitude' and '34691 does not mention attitude or link to 22706'. They are probably right for these short circulars, but they must be worded as 'not in the accessible snippet text', not as facts about the full documents. The same goes for 'no public technical explanation was found': with GCN, swift.gsfc, ADS and arXiv all blocked, it holds only for that search.

(3) Two smaller generalizations. 'BAT flight software is C++ on VxWorks on a RAD6000' generalizes from the RAD6000's software, while a separate 21020 DSP handles imaging, and the description is a 2004 pre-launch one. 'In BAT software' fits 22706, 21077 and 20555 ('Swift/BAT' or 'BAT onboard'), but 32397, 34691 and 43470 say only 'onboard' or 'the software'. Calling 21077 'an earlier instance' is true, but 19982 (2016-10-04) and 20555 (2017-01-28) come earlier, so the recurrence goes back at least to 2016.

The core conclusion still holds: Swift should be cited as a non-cFS example, with the attitude wording limited to 22706. Because the literal 'no source links Swift/BAT to cFS' statement is contradicted by a primary source, I mark the claim refuted and give the narrower wording above. I could not open any GCN page, any arXiv or NTRS PDF, ADS, or archive.org. Every GCN and paper statement above therefore rests on search snippets, except the cFE heritage slide text, which I read in full as OCR.
